draft.title: Straight-line depreciation
card: Straight-line depreciation charges the same amount of depreciation expense in every year of an asset's useful life.
Residual value is the amount the business expects the asset to be worth at the end of its useful life. The depreciable amount is cost less residual value.
Annual depreciation = (cost - residual value) ÷ useful life in years.
Example: a machine costs $50 000, has a residual value of $10 000 and a useful life of 5 years. Annual depreciation = $40 000 ÷ 5 = $8 000.
draft.remember: Straight-line: take off the residual value first, then divide by the years.

a.q: A printer costs $12 000, has a residual value of $2 000 and a useful life of 5 years. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
a.why: Depreciable amount = $12 000 - $2 000 = $10 000. Dividing by 5 years gives $2 000 a year. $2 400 is wrong because it divides the full cost and ignores the residual value.
a.clue: Subtract the residual value before you divide.

b.q: Priya's bakery in Ballarat buys an oven for $30 000 and pays $2 000 to install it. It has a useful life of 4 years and a residual value of $4 000. What is the annual straight-line depreciation?
b.why: The oven is recorded at $32 000, which is the price plus installation. Less the $4 000 residual value, the depreciable amount is $28 000, and $28 000 ÷ 4 = $7 000. $6 500 is wrong because it leaves out the installation cost.
b.clue: Work out the total cost of the oven first, then subtract the residual value.

problems.detail: Question b depends on knowing that installation is part of an asset's cost. The card never teaches this, and it belongs to point 1 (Valuing a non-current asset). A student who only read this card could pick $6 500, and the why explains point 1's idea here instead of only mentioning it.

check.summary: Both answers check out ($2 000 and $7 000). Question b needs installation to be counted in cost, which this card does not teach and which belongs to point 1, so the oven should be given at a single total cost.
